scenes.title: Nexo can talk, but not act

sentences.text: Week four at Contoso.
An employee writes: the V P N steps did not work, please open a ticket.
Nexo found the right guide, but now it is stuck.
It can only say: please call the help desk.
The employee closes the chat, annoyed.
Nexo can read, but it cannot act.
Knowledge is what the agent reads.
Tools are what the agent does.
Today we give Nexo hands, and the adapters that connect them to real systems.
A tool is a capability the agent can run: read an email, create a ticket, check an inventory.
Think of the apps installed on the agent's phone.
The main types are a connector, an agent flow, a prompt, a REST A P I, an M C P server, and computer use.
With generative orchestration, the agent chooses a tool by its name and description.
In classic mode, a tool is only called from a topic.
The most common tool is a connector.
Picture a travel plug adapter.
Your device always has the same plug, and the adapter makes it fit in every country.
A connector is a wrapper around an A P I.
It translates the agent's calls into the language of each service, like SharePoint, Outlook or Salesforce, and it comes with ready-made actions.
The same connectors work in Copilot Studio, Power Automate, Power Apps and Azure Logic Apps.
Connectors come in three kinds.
Standard ones, like SharePoint, are included in every Copilot Studio plan.
Premium ones are only available in certain plans.
Custom ones you build yourself, usually from an OpenAPI specification, when a service has no ready connector.
Watch one trap: the Copilot Studio plan for Teams does not allow premium connectors.
And administrators use data policies to allow or block connectors, custom connectors and M C P servers included.
Your turn.
Contoso's H R team builds an agent with the Copilot Studio plan for Teams, included in Microsoft three sixty five.
The agent needs a premium connector for the payroll system.
What happens?
They need a plan with premium connectors?
It works, as all connectors are included?
Or it works once an admin data policy allows it?
Decide before I answer.
They need a plan with premium connectors.
The Teams plan does not allow premium ones, and a data policy cannot grant a license.
A connector needs a connection: saved credentials for a service.
By default, it uses the credentials of the person chatting, so each employee signs in once and acts with their own permissions.
The alternative is maker provided credentials, which need an authenticated channel.
Use them with care: every user then acts with the permissions of the person who set up the tool.
Connections can be shared from the Power Apps portal, in Connections, with the Can use and share permission.
Your turn.
I T purchase approvals live in an internal system.
It has its own A P I and an OpenAPI description, but no ready connector.
How does Nexo get a tool for it?
Use computer use to click through its screens?
Build a custom connector from its OpenAPI?
Or add the system's website as a knowledge source?
Decide before I answer.
Build a custom connector.
The A P I exists, so you wrap it.
Computer use is for systems that only have a screen.

scenes.title: Add a connector in the studio

sentences.text: Let's add one in the studio.
Open Nexo and go to the Tools page.
Select Add a tool, then Connector.
Search for the service and choose the action, like create a ticket.
If there is no connection yet, select Create new connection and sign in.
Select Add and configure, then improve the tool's name and description.
Finally, test a request in the test pane and watch the activity map show the tool running.
Back to week four.
The team added the help desk's premium connector, and a developer built a custom connector for purchase approvals from its OpenAPI.
The admins checked the data policies, so both are allowed.
The same employee writes again.
Nexo signs them in once and opens the ticket with their own credentials.
Remember: premium needs the right plan, no connector means a custom one, and data policies decide what is allowed.
Next, where all of this lives: environments.
